newsitem.title: FRANCE: Frenchman denounces wartime collaborators careers.
newsitem.headline: Frenchman denounces wartime collaborators careers.

text.p: The forthcoming trial of Maurice Papon for crimes against humanity underlines the fact that many officials in France's collaborationist World War Two government pursued post-war careers unchallenged, a researcher said.

Michel Slitinsky, who played a major part in bringing Papon to trial, told Reuters that 52 former ministers in the Vichy government escaped prosecution in the post-war purges and trials of suspected collaborators.

He said 375 prefects (regional government representatives), deputy prefects and chief aides in the pro-Nazi administration played on old boys' networks in the civil service to follow their careers after the war ended.

Papon, 87, was a case in point. As secretary general of the Bordeaux administration during the war, he was in charge of "Jewish issues", but he said later he had belonged to two anti-Nazi Resistance groups.

General Charles de Gaulle made him a prefect, opening the way to his rise to chief administrator of Corsica, secretary general of the Moroccan protectorate, Paris police chief, member of parliament, budget minister and a Legion of Honour award.

Papon has argued that he helped the Resistance, saved several Jews and watered down the Vichy government's harshest orders. Were it not for the chance finding of wartime files in an attic in 1981, he would have enjoyed a quiet retirement.
After 15 years of legal wrangling, the supreme court last week ordered him to stand trial for crimes against humanity on charges of sending more than 1,500 Jews to Nazi death camps.

They included the family of Slitinsky, who narrowly escaped the French police raid himself by hiding on his house's roof. He has devoted much of his life to finding out what happened to Vichy officials and how some evaded the post-war purges.
"It is obvious that the instructions given by (de Gaulle's) provisional government and the National Resistance Council to purge civil servants compromised since 1940 were not carried out," he said.

As France was liberated, tens of thousands of people suspected of collaborating with the Nazis were shot in summary executions and up to 300,000 were jailed. Hundreds of thousands were sacked, retired or demoted in their jobs.
A special high court condemned 18 former senior officials to death and 25 to prison or forced labour. Three, including former Vichy prime minister Pierre Laval, were executed.
But Slitinsky said many Vichy officials secured fake certificates clearing them of collaboration with the German occupying forces.

He cited the Official Gazette of March 26, 1954, as listing 42 Vichy officials purges who were later reintegrated into the civil service, 42 who were kept on in the civil service without a job and 36 who were detached to other services.

Slitinsky said he had reconstituted the post-war careers of some of 28 officials in Vichy prefects' offices who were singled out in alleged documents from the German Abwehr intelligence service for noted cooperation with German authorities.

He said one of them was deputy prefect in northern France in 1945, prefect in central France in 1954, official in Algeria in 1958 before it became independent, again prefect in central France in 1964, adviser in a state aeronautical firm, then chief aide to the mayor and MP of a central French city.
He said another rose from deputy prefect in western France in 1945 to chief aide of a junior minister, adviser at the Interior Ministry in 1958 and member of the National Assembly.
